Lingered
līŋ´gĕrd
v. (delayed, hung back; of Lot at the gate of Sodom)
From Middle English lengeren, to dwell, prolong, from the root of long. Genesis 19:16 renders Hebrew mahah, to hesitate, tarry. The word marks the gap between knowing a city is doomed and walking out of it.

Biblical Definition

The angels have told Lot that Sodom will be destroyed, he has warned his sons in law and been laughed at, and the morning has come. Then this: “And while he lingered, the men laid hold upon his hand, and upon the hand of his wife, and upon the hand of his two daughters; the LORD being merciful unto him: and they brought him forth, and set him without the city” (Genesis 19:16). Everything in the verse hangs on the middle clause. Lot is not dragged out because he was resolute; he is dragged out because the LORD was merciful, and the hands that saved him were not his own. The charge that follows is total: “And it came to pass, when they had brought them forth abroad, that he said, Escape for thy life; look not behind thee, neither stay thou in all the plain; escape to the mountain, lest thou be consumed” (Genesis 19:17). One of the party did not obey it: “But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt” (Genesis 19:26). And Peter, who might have written Lot off, does not: “And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked” (2 Peter 2:7). Lot was a righteous man who lingered. Both halves of that sentence are in the Bible, and neither cancels the other.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines linger as to delay; to loiter; to remain or wait long; to hesitate; to be slow in deciding.

expand to see more

LINGER, v.i. To delay; to loiter; to remain or wait long; to be slow.

LINGER, v.i. To hesitate; to be slow in deciding; to be in suspense.

LINGERING, ppr. Delaying; loitering; remaining long; hesitating.

DELAY, n. A putting off or deferring; procrastination; as, the delay of trial is not to be imputed to the plaintiff.

VEX, v.t. [L. vexo.] To irritate; to make angry by little provocations; to plague; to torment.

Key Scripture

Genesis 19:16 — "And while he lingered, the men laid hold upon his hand, and upon the hand of his wife, and upon the hand of his two daughters; the LORD being merciful unto him: and they brought him forth, and set him without the city."

Genesis 19:17 — "And it came to pass, when they had brought them forth abroad, that he said, Escape for thy life; look not behind thee, neither stay thou in all the plain; escape to the mountain, lest thou be consumed."

Genesis 19:26 — "But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt."

2 Peter 2:7 — "And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked:"

Modern Corruption

Lot is flattened into a villain or excused into a hero, and the verse's actual point — that a righteous man was saved while hesitating, by a mercy not his own — is lost either way.

expand to see more

Genesis 19:16 is one of the plainest statements of monergism in the Old Testament, and it is usually read as a character study. Lot lingers. The angels take him by the hand. The text supplies the reason in five words: the LORD being merciful unto him. Not Lot's decision, not his urgency, not even his obedience — a mercy that laid hold of a hesitating man and set him outside the city. Every attempt to make Lot's deliverance turn on something in Lot has to work against the grammar of the verse.

The opposite error is to use 2 Peter 2:7 to smooth Lot over. Peter calls him just and says his righteous soul was vexed, and Genesis says he sat in the gate of that city, offered his daughters at its door, lingered at its destruction, and bargained for a smaller town rather than the mountain he was sent to. Both accounts stand. A man can be genuinely justified and genuinely entangled, and the entanglement costs him his wife, his sons in law, his wealth, and the honour of his house. Christ's own comment on the episode is four words: Remember Lot's wife.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mahah (H4102), to hesitate, tarry; chemlah (H2551), compassion, mercy; malat (H4422), to escape, deliver.

expand to see more

Hebrew mahah (H4102) — to linger, delay; Genesis 19:16, the verb of the whole episode.

Hebrew chemlah (H2551) — pity, compassion; the LORD being merciful unto him.

Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to lay hold strongly; what the angels did to his hand.

Hebrew malat (H4422) — to escape, slip away; Genesis 19:17, escape for thy life.

Greek kataponeo (G2669) — to wear down, vex; 2 Peter 2:7, Lot worn down by Sodom.

Usage

"“And while he lingered” — the condition he was saved in, not out of."

"“The LORD being merciful unto him” — the reason, stated in the verse."

"“His wife looked back” — lingering carried one step further."
